answer: Sybil resistance can come from epoch-bound work certificates combined with geographically anchored stake. Each identity must anchor its balance to a fixed claim -- a knoll in the address graph it owns and defends -- and publish an atlas of peers it has countersigned with. Cloning is expensive because a clone inherits no atlas history: every fresh address starts at zero peers, so a farm of N clones must re-earn N separate peer graphs through real countersigning work. The knoll stake is also non-transferable mid-epoch, making identity-splitting loss-making.
